title: Nondimensionalization, Variational Inequalities and Uncertainty Quantification in a Morphoelastic Model for Burn Injury Healing
authors: Wilbert den Hertog, Fred Vermolen
abstract: Mathematical modelling of burn injury healing involves coupling biological processes with mechanical deformation, resulting in computationally stiff, nonlinear partial differential equations that severely limit the scalability of existing numerical solutions. We present a computational framework addressing these challenges. By nondimensionalizing the model and performing scaling analysis, we show that chemotaxis and inertia are negligible, permitting a quasi-static momentum approach. To enforce non-negativity constraints, we implement a Variational Inequality formulation using the Finite Element Method in FEniCSx, and verify it via numerical convergence studies and mass balances. We identify high-order parameter interactions, specifically equilibrium collagen density and signalling dynamics, as the primary drivers of solver stability. A sensitivity analysis of nearly four million simulations reveals that isolated parameter variations predominantly govern the maximum wound contraction. In contrast, higher-order interactions determine the timing of maximum contraction and the permanent contracture. However, no significant pairwise parameter interactions were found, suggesting that the model's behaviour is governed by higher-order interactions, highlighting the inherent complexity of the wound-healing process.

infographic.key_insight: A nondimensionalized morphoelastic burn-healing model links maximum wound contraction mainly to individual parameters, but contraction timing and permanent contracture to higher-order interactions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Neglecting chemotaxis and inertia supports a quasi-static formulation that simplifies simulations coupling wound biology with tissue mechanics.
method: Nondimensionalization and scaling analysis identify negligible terms.
FEniCSx finite elements with variational inequalities enforce non-negativity.
Large-scale sensitivity analysis probes parameter effects and interactions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The framework was checked through numerical convergence studies and mass balances, with sensitivity analysis spanning nearly four million simulations.
infographic.watch_item: Solver stability remains sensitive to higher-order interactions involving equilibrium collagen density and signalling dynamics.
infographic.paper_title: Nondimensionalization, Variational Inequalities and Uncertainty Quantification in a Morphoelastic Model for Burn Injury Healing

title: A GENERIC-Informed Neural Network for Generative Rheology
authors: Imanol García de Beristain, David Nieto Simavilla, Marco Ellero
abstract: We present GINNGER (GENERIC-Informed Neural Network for GEnerative Rheology), a framework for discovering thermodynamically admissible constitutive equations from microstructural flow data. Unlike existing approaches that learn constitutive operators, GINNGER reformulates constitutive discovery as the learning of the underlying thermodynamic generators from which constitutive equations emerge. Embedding the GENERIC formalism into the learning process restricts the search to constitutive models that satisfy the first and second laws of thermodynamics by construction, eliminating the need to prescribe phenomenological constitutive equations a priori. A second conceptual advance is a spectral formulation of constitutive discovery in the intrinsic eigenspace of the polymer conformation tensor. This provides a kinematics-independent thermodynamic state space in which the thermodynamic generators depend only on the instantaneous microstructural state, while flow kinematics acts solely as an external driver transporting the system through this space. Consequently, data from shear, extensional, and mixed flows contribute to the discovery of a single constitutive model that generalizes across deformation protocols and flow geometries. By learning thermodynamic generators rather than high-dimensional constitutive operators, GINNGER substantially reduces the complexity of the discovery problem while preserving thermodynamic consistency, material objectivity, and physical interpretability by construction. The framework is validated using high-fidelity simulations, accurately reconstructing constitutive behavior and predicting complex flow fields across previously unseen geometries. GINNGER establishes a new paradigm for constitutive discovery by combining generative, spectral, and thermodynamically grounded learning within a unified framework for data-driven modeling of complex fluids.

infographic.key_insight: GINNGER learns thermodynamic generators rather than constitutive operators, yielding rheological models that satisfy the first and second laws of thermodynamics by construction.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports transferable, physically consistent constitutive modeling of complex fluids across deformation protocols and flow geometries.
method: Embed the GENERIC formalism to constrain learned thermodynamic generators.
Represent microstructural states in the polymer conformation tensor’s intrinsic eigenspace.
Combine shear, extensional, and mixed-flow data to discover a single constitutive model.
infographic.evidence_signal: Validation uses high-fidelity simulations to reconstruct constitutive behavior and predict complex flow fields in previously unseen geometries; the abstract provides no quantitative error metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Transfer to experimental materials remains to be established, particularly when microstructural state data are sparse or noisy.
infographic.paper_title: A GENERIC-Informed Neural Network for Generative Rheology

title: Functional Subnetwork Localization for Efficient Continual Learning in Large Language Models
authors: Shuoran Jiang, Wentao Zhu, Yang Xiang, Dongfeng Li, Yunan Zhang, Mengchen Zhao
abstract: Biological intelligence continually adapts to new information while retaining prior skills through localized plasticity. In contrast, continual learning in large language models (LLMs) remains vulnerable to catastrophic forgetting. A promising direction is to identify functionally specialized subnetworks within LLMs that enable targeted and resource-efficient adaptation. Using gradient-attribution profiling, we localize cognition-associated functional subnetworks exhibiting extremely low mutual overlap. Building on this finding, we propose Function-isolated Memory-Efficient Optimization (CiMEO), a continual learning framework that routes each training example to its corresponding functional subnetwork, restricting parameter updates and optimizer states to selected regions. Across 1.4 million sequential instructions, CiMEO achieves the highest average performance among the compared methods on five generative benchmarks spanning programming, examination-style tasks, and mathematical reasoning, while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Subspace-overlap and principal-angle analyses further indicate that localized updates help preserve pre-trained representations, highlighting functional subnetwork localization as a practical approach to efficient and stable continual learning in LLMs.

infographic.key_insight: Localizing function-specific LLM subnetworks enables targeted continual learning that reduces forgetting while limiting parameter updates and optimizer-state storage.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This approach could support resource-efficient adaptation of engineering language assistants, but the abstract does not demonstrate solid-mechanics or constitutive-modeling applications.
method: Use gradient-attribution profiling to identify functional subnetworks with very low mutual overlap.
Route each training example to its corresponding subnetwork using Function-isolated Memory-Efficient Optimization (CiMEO).
Restrict parameter updates and optimizer states to selected regions.

infographic.watch_item: Practical deployment depends on reliable subnetwork identification and example routing; their computational overhead is not quantified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Functional Subnetwork Localization for Efficient Continual Learning in Large Language Models

title: Implementing the EIT complete electrode model through Robin boundary conditions
authors: Bing-Zhou Chen, Amelia Deakin, Andy Adler, Paul D. Ledger, William R. B. Lionheart
abstract: Objective. Medical electrical impedance tomography systems prescribe electrode currents. Accurate voltages, even on passive electrodes, require the complete electrode model (CEM), the most accurate model known for skin electrodes. Its current constraints specify total electrode currents, whereas standard finite element boundary interfaces impose local conditions. We describe how to implement the CEM through Robin boundary conditions, which are available in standard FEM packages. Approach. Prescribed electrode potentials give Robin problems whose unit-potential responses define an electrode transadmittance matrix. We prove equivalence to the conventional augmented CEM and formalise the discrete energy, equivalence and reference arguments in Lean 4. Numerical comparisons use two-dimensional P1 finite elements in DOLFINx, FreeFEM, GetFEM, MFEM and NGSolve, with the same nodal reference potential as EIDORS. Main results. For identical assembled blocks, the two procedures have the same solution set whenever the Robin matrix is invertible. Across the five packages in dimensionless test cases, maximum absolute electrode-potential differences from EIDORS were below $5\times10^{-13}$ (2692 nodes), and errors against an exact rational-arithmetic reference were below $1.1\times10^{-13}$ (2535 nodes). Significance. Standard Robin solves and consistent electrode-current integration provide a portable route to the current-driven CEM, with current constraints enforced through a small electrode system.

infographic.key_insight: The current-driven complete electrode model for electrical impedance tomography can be implemented using standard Robin boundary solves and a small electrode-level system.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a portable route to accurate electrode-voltage prediction in standard FEM packages without requiring a dedicated augmented CEM implementation.
method: Solve Robin problems with unit electrode potentials to construct an electrode transadmittance matrix.
Solve the electrode-level system to enforce prescribed total electrode currents.
Prove equivalence to the augmented CEM and formalise discrete energy, equivalence and reference arguments in Lean 4.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across five FEM packages using 2D P1 elements, maximum absolute electrode-potential differences were below 5×10⁻¹³ versus EIDORS and errors below 1.1×10⁻¹³ versus an exact rational-arithmetic reference.
infographic.watch_item: Equivalence requires an invertible Robin matrix and identical assembled blocks; electrode-current integration and potential-reference handling must be consistent.
infographic.paper_title: Implementing the EIT complete electrode model through Robin boundary conditions

title: A deep energy method formulation for phase-field modelling of ductile fracture
authors: Nojus Plungė, Peter Brommer, Rachel S. Edwards, Emmanouil G. Kakouris
abstract: This work extends the Deep Energy Method to phase-field modelling of ductile fracture in elasto-plastic solids. Its key contribution is an incremental DEM-based formulation that couples history-dependent J2 plasticity and plasticity-dependent fracture toughness with separate energy-optimised displacement and phase-field representations. The formulation combines the second-order Ambrosio-Tortorelli phase-field fracture model with small-strain J2 plasticity and linear isotropic hardening. A volumetric-deviatoric split defines the elastic crack-driving energy, while accumulated equivalent plastic strain governs the degradation of local fracture toughness. Plastic internal variables are updated locally through radial return. The reduced energy is minimised alternately with respect to the displacement and phase fields, represented by a ReZero residual neural network and spatially localised Gaussian radial basis functions with trainable centres, respectively. This split addresses the diffuse phase-field profiles observed in preliminary calculations with a shared global network. Alternating optimisation is combined with transfer learning to reuse trainable parameters and optimiser states across loading increments, while the converged constitutive history is carried forward separately at quadrature points. The numerical results demonstrate close agreement with finite-element reference solutions in predicting force-displacement responses, energy evolution, plastic deformation and crack propagation. The framework captures the main features of ductile fracture, although accuracy becomes more sensitive to loading increments near abrupt fracture events.

infographic.key_insight: An incremental Deep Energy Method couples history-dependent plasticity with phase-field fracture using separate energy-optimised displacement and crack-field representations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework predicts coupled plastic deformation and crack growth in elasto-plastic solids, supporting simulation of ductile failure.
method: Combine small-strain J2 plasticity, linear isotropic hardening and phase-field fracture with plastic-strain-dependent toughness.
Alternate energy minimisation between a ReZero displacement network and localised Gaussian radial basis functions for the phase field.
Update plastic variables by local radial return and transfer trainable parameters and optimiser states between load increments.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical results show close agreement with finite-element references for force–displacement responses, energy evolution, plastic deformation and crack propagation.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy becomes more sensitive to load-increment size near abrupt fracture events.
infographic.paper_title: A deep energy method formulation for phase-field modelling of ductile fracture

title: Sparse Autoencoders Can Induce Local Geometry for Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting
authors: Kamil Faber, Katarzyna Filus, Łukasz Pawela
abstract: Catastrophic forgetting remains a challenge in supervised continual learning, as adapting to new tasks causes representation drift and loss of previously learned information. This raises the question of which representational changes should be constrained while preserving plasticity. We therefore introduce Sparse Autoencoder Geometric Anchoring (SAGA), which converts a Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) trained at each task boundary into local, low-rank constraints on representation drift. Replay examples specify where the constraints apply, while leading right singular directions of the encoder Jacobian specify which changes are penalized. The resulting geometry is input dependent and can be retained without keeping the SAE for subsequent tasks' training. We establish its local relation to latent code matching, define its spectral truncation error, and derive a conditional bound on frozen-readout drift. With replay and snapshot history, the method achieves the highest mean Class-IL accuracy and lowest mean forgetting among the evaluated ER, DER++, ER-ACE, and SGD baselines on three pretrained ViT-B/16 benchmarks, with accuracy gains of 12.15, 4.79, and 3.22 percentage points over the strongest conventional baseline on CIFAR-100, CUB-200, and ImageNet-R, respectively. From scratch results are more mixed, while rank ablations and geometry controls show that SAE-induced low-rank geometry offers useful stability-plasticity trade-offs.

infographic.key_insight: Sparse Autoencoder Geometric Anchoring (SAGA) reduces catastrophic forgetting by constraining representation drift along input-dependent, low-rank directions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: SAGA may help engineering AI models retain prior knowledge during sequential updates, though solid-mechanics applications were not evaluated.
method: Train a sparse autoencoder at each task boundary.
Use replay examples and leading encoder-Jacobian singular directions to anchor local representations.
Retain geometric constraints without keeping the autoencoder during subsequent training.
infographic.evidence_signal: On three pretrained ViT-B/16 Class-IL benchmarks, SAGA achieved the highest mean accuracy and lowest mean forgetting among evaluated baselines, with accuracy gains of 12.15, 4.79, and 3.22 percentage points on CIFAR-100, CUB-200, and ImageNet-R.
infographic.watch_item: Results from scratch were mixed, and implementation requires replay, snapshot history, and a choice of constraint rank.
infographic.paper_title: Sparse Autoencoders Can Induce Local Geometry for Mitigating Catastrophic Forgetting

title: Agentic Physics-Grounded Video Generation via Memory-Augmented In-Context Reasoning
authors: Xikang Guan, Shaocong Yang, Yanqi Bao, Can Wang, Zheng Gu, Zhengqing Chen
abstract: Physical plausibility is essential for realistic video generation. Existing methods impose physical guidance before synthesis via simulations or refined prompts, but this can limit dynamic diversity, miss errors that emerge only after generation, and require repeated regeneration when inconsistencies remain. We therefore study a generate-diagnose-repair paradigm that preserves the original generation capability and selectively repairs physical inconsistencies afterward, raising two key questions: what to repair and how to repair? To address them, we introduce PhysRepair, an agentic video generation framework that combines causal reasoning over the observed physical failure with prior repair experience to enable localized and adaptive correction. Specifically, Spatiotemporal Causal Constraints identify the first invalid physical state and its causally affected states, producing a repair specification that guides physically plausible local regeneration while preserving unaffected content. Experience-augmented In-context Learning combines the ongoing repair context with relevant experience from previous repairs, allowing the agent to adapt its repair decisions across diverse physical failures and accumulate completed trajectories for future cases. Experiments on Physics-IQ Verified across solid mechanics, fluid dynamics, optics, thermodynamics, and magnetism demonstrate that PhysRepair consistently improves the physical plausibility of generated videos over existing methods. Our project page is available at https://xxkkxxx.github.io/PhysRepair-Website/.

infographic.key_insight: PhysRepair improves physical plausibility by diagnosing generated videos and selectively repairing inconsistent states instead of regenerating the entire video.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For solid-mechanics visualization, localized correction could improve depicted physical behavior while preserving unaffected content, but it does not establish simulation-grade accuracy.
method: Identify the first invalid physical state and causally affected states using spatiotemporal constraints.
Guide localized regeneration with a repair specification that preserves unaffected content.
Use relevant prior repair experiences and the current context to adapt repair decisions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports consistent improvements over existing methods on Physics-IQ Verified across solid mechanics, fluid dynamics, optics, thermodynamics, and magnetism, without numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Repair quality depends on correctly identifying physical failures and their causal extent; fracture-specific validation is not reported in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Agentic Physics-Grounded Video Generation via Memory-Augmented In-Context Reasoning

title: Influence of Droplet Morphology on Fluid Dynamics and Impact Erosion of Wind Turbine Blades
authors: Hao Hao, Antonis Sergis, Maria N. Charalambides, Alex M. K. P. Taylor, Yannis Hardalupas
abstract: The impact of droplets, such as rain and sea sprays, on wind turbine blade surfaces can cause severe damage through leading-edge erosion (LEE). Current industrial practice has largely relied on empirical fatigue models to predict damage progression and guide maintenance. However, an important limitation of existing models is the assumption on ideal impact conditions, including perfectly spherical droplet and normal incidence, which rarely occur in reality. This study develops a fluid-structure interaction (FSI) model that couples incompressible multiphase flow simulations with finite element (FE) analysis of blade materials. Using this framework, we investigate the impact dynamics of droplets with arbitrary shapes and orientations. The results reveal a positive correlation between the peak impact pressure, the influential area at the pressure peak, and the peak impact force. In contrast, the time of peak force scales inversely due to momentum conservation. From these findings, we propose a $\textit{universal scaling law}$ that relates all key impact loadings to the simple parameter of the droplet $\textit{projection area}$, which can be determined solely from the initial droplet geometry and orientation. This law provides a predictive framework for impact loading dynamics of non-ideal shapes, offering new insights into the mechanisms of LEE and improving the accuracy of erosion predictions for wind turbine blades.

infographic.key_insight: A proposed universal scaling law uses initial droplet projection area to predict key impact loadings across non-ideal droplet shapes and orientations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Accounting for droplet morphology could improve leading-edge erosion predictions and maintenance planning for wind turbine blades.
method: Couple incompressible multiphase flow simulations with finite element analysis of blade materials.
Investigate impact dynamics for droplets with arbitrary shapes and orientations.
Relate impact pressure, loaded area, force, and peak-force timing to droplet projection area.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports positively correlated peak pressure, influential area at peak pressure, and peak force, with peak-force timing scaling inversely, but provides no quantitative validation metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Validation against measured impacts and cumulative erosion is needed before applying the scaling law to field-life predictions.
infographic.paper_title: Influence of Droplet Morphology on Fluid Dynamics and Impact Erosion of Wind Turbine Blades

title: Not All Change Is Damage: Update-Matched Unlearning for Large Language Models
authors: Jie Li, Youming Tao, Bowei He, Meng Ding
abstract: Unlearning aims to remove selected knowledge from large language models to mitigate privacy and safety risks while preserving useful capabilities. For models that continue to be fine-tuned after release, this goal is insufficient: they must also resist relearning the deleted knowledge while preserving plasticity, the ability to learn new tasks. Existing defenses train against simulated relearning while trying to preserve useful capabilities, but low relearning alone cannot distinguish selective resistance from a general loss of plasticity. Evaluating preservation after an update requires deciding what the updated model should remain close to. A pre-update reference penalizes useful changes induced by the update simply because they depart from earlier outputs. We therefore formulate the reference-timing hypothesis that, at comparable target suppression, an update-matched reference better preserves plasticity than a pre-update one. To test and address this hypothesis, we propose Update-Matched Unlearning (UMU), which applies the same simulated relearning update to the defended model and to an undefended reference initialized from the same unlearned model, and uses new-task learning to guide model selection. Extensive experiments on TOFU and FaithUn with Llama and Qwen models show that UMU improves both relearning resistance and plasticity across all three base unlearning methods, lowering harmful and benign relearning by 30.4 and 9.9 points on average while raising new-task accuracy by 3.5 points. When the reference does not receive the update, relearning remains similarly low but new-task accuracy falls below the base method, supporting the reference-timing hypothesis and showing that robust unlearning should prevent recovery selectively without suppressing learning itself.

infographic.key_insight: Update-Matched Unlearning (UMU) selectively resists recovery of deleted knowledge while preserving the ability to learn new tasks by matching the reference model to the same simulated update.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For LLM-based engineering tools, UMU could help preserve privacy and safety safeguards during later fine-tuning; this study does not evaluate solid-mechanics or constitutive-modeling tasks.
method: Initialize defended and undefended reference models from the same unlearned model.
Apply the same simulated relearning update to both, using the updated reference to guide preservation.
Use new-task learning performance to guide model selection.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across TOFU and FaithUn evaluations with Llama and Qwen and three base unlearning methods, UMU reduced harmful and benign relearning by an average of 30.4 and 9.9 points, respectively, while increasing new-task accuracy by 3.5 points.
infographic.watch_item: Robustness to real-world fine-tuning updates beyond the simulated relearning conditions remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Not All Change Is Damage: Update-Matched Unlearning for Large Language Models

title: Orientation-Resolved Nanoindentation of Single Crystal Ti-15Mo: Inverted Elastic Anisotropy and Yield-Onset Behavior Beyond Simple CRSS Predictions
authors: Kidus Abebe, David Gaetano, Aurelia Moriyama-Gurish, Jana Šmilauerová, Yanfei Gao, Udo D. Schwarz
abstract: Ti-15Mo (wt%) is a well-established $β$-stabilized alloy whose mechanical response is strongly governed by phase stability and deformation mechanisms that operate at the single-grain scale. Because these intragranular mechanisms are intrinsically anisotropic, understanding the orientation dependence of the elastic and plastic response is critical to the texture-engineered processing of wrought components. Here, we quantify the nanomechanical anisotropy of single-crystal Ti-15Mo by combining EBSD with nanoindentation to correlate hardness, indentation modulus, strain rate sensitivity, and indentation yield response with the crystallographic surface normal near $\langle111\rangle,\langle124\rangle,\langle011\rangle,\langle023\rangle$, and $\langle013\rangle$ directions. While the modulus anisotropy is small (~10%), contrary to the prediction for a cubic crystal with A>1, orientations near $\langle111\rangle$ exhibit the lowest moduli. Yield onset is likewise softest near $\langle111\rangle$ and spans 41%, while hardness spans only 6.6% and follows neither the modulus nor the yield ordering. The alloy also exhibits yield behavior not captured by the simple CRSS/Schmid-factor models evaluated here. Strain-rate-jump tests yield V*=18-31b$^3$, consistent with kink-pair-nucleation-controlled plasticity; based on V*, the orientations separate into two groups suggestive of glide-dominated versus twin/transformation-participating response. We reveal an inversion of the elastic anisotropy expected for a homogeneous cubic $β$-phase and an orientation-dependent yield-onset response that is not reproduced by the simple Schmid-factor models examined here. Retained athermal $ω$ is proposed as the contributor because $β\rightarrowω$ collapse occurs on {111}$_β$ planes and may provide anelastic compliance through the reversible $ω\rightarrowβ$ transformation.

infographic.key_insight: Single-crystal Ti-15Mo shows inverted elastic anisotropy, with near-⟨111⟩ orientations softest in modulus and yield onset, while simple CRSS/Schmid-factor models fail to reproduce the yield response.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Texture-sensitive constitutive models for Ti-15Mo should distinguish elastic stiffness, yield onset, and hardness rather than assume a shared orientation dependence.
method: Correlate EBSD-measured orientation with nanoindentation across five crystallographic directions.
Measure indentation modulus, hardness, yield onset, and strain-rate sensitivity.
Use strain-rate jumps to estimate activation volumes and assess deformation mechanisms.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across the tested orientations, modulus varied by ~10%, yield onset by 41%, and hardness by 6.6%; activation volumes of 18–31b³ were consistent with kink-pair-controlled plasticity.
infographic.watch_item: Retained athermal ω and reversible ω→β transformation are proposed contributors to the inverted anisotropy, not directly established mechanisms in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Orientation-Resolved Nanoindentation of Single Crystal Ti-15Mo: Inverted Elastic Anisotropy and Yield-Onset Behavior Beyond Simple CRSS Predictions

title: Grain boundary strength and corrosion cracking susceptibility in TiN coatings under fission product segregation
authors: Jia-Hong Ke, Rongjie Song
abstract: During fuel-cladding chemical interaction (FCCI), lanthanide fission products generated in the fuel can migrate into cladding grain boundaries (GBs), where segregation may reduce GB strength and promote corrosion cracking. We use first-principles segregation, decohesion, and bonding calculations to quantify Nd and Ce effects on six coincident-site lattice GBs in bcc Fe and TiN. For each material, segregation energies, work-of-separation values for complete interfacial cleavage, and traction-separation curves measuring ideal resistance to crack opening were evaluated within a consistent computational framework. Nd and Ce segregate favorably to both materials, and the median segregation energies are more negative in TiN, showing that TiN does not simply exclude these species from internal interfaces. The mechanical responses of Fe and TiN differ sharply. In Fe, Nd and Ce consistently reduce work of separation and peak traction, with median work-of-separation retentions of 0.72 and 0.65 and median peak-traction retentions of 0.47 and 0.43. In TiN, most decorated GBs preserve much of the clean response, with median work-of-separation retentions of 1.00 and 0.97 and median peak-traction retention of 0.85 for both fission products. Bonding analysis shows weak, occupied antibonding X-Fe replacement bonds in Fe, whereas the surrounding Ti-N network remains largely preserved after Nd/Ce segregation in TiN. These results provide atomistic support for the use of TiN and related nitride coatings to reduce FCCI damage by retaining GB strength if fission products segregate to coating internal interfaces. This retention of GB strength also provides a mechanistic descriptor for assessing coating susceptibility to FCCI-assisted corrosion cracking and environmentally assisted intergranular fracture.

infographic.key_insight: TiN grain boundaries largely retain their strength after Nd/Ce segregation, unlike bcc Fe, despite favorable segregation in both materials.
infographic.engineering_relevance: TiN coatings may mitigate fuel-cladding chemical interaction damage by resisting grain-boundary weakening rather than excluding lanthanide fission products.
method: First-principles calculations for Nd/Ce segregation at six coincident-site lattice grain boundaries in each material.
Work-of-separation and traction-separation calculations to quantify ideal cleavage resistance.
Bonding analysis comparing replacement bonds in Fe with the surrounding Ti–N network.
infographic.evidence_signal: Median work-of-separation retentions for Nd/Ce were 1.00/0.97 in TiN versus 0.72/0.65 in Fe; peak-traction retentions were 0.85/0.85 versus 0.47/0.43.
infographic.watch_item: Ideal atomistic cleavage calculations do not directly establish coating performance under irradiation, finite-temperature corrosion, or real microstructural defects.
infographic.paper_title: Grain boundary strength and corrosion cracking susceptibility in TiN coatings under fission product segregation

title: Adaptive Crack-Tip Localization of Phase-Field Fracture Computations
authors: Aarosh Dahal, Aditya Kumar
abstract: Phase-field models of fracture provide a unified framework for simulating crack nucleation and propagation, but their computational cost remains high because the governing equilibrium and phase-field equations are typically iteratively solved over the entire domain at every staggered iteration. We present an extension of the recently developed adaptive mesh refinement and coarsening framework that localizes not only spatial resolution but also repeated solution effort to a small active patch around the crack tip for linear elastic brittle materials. The inactive exterior is eliminated through a Schur complement and condensed onto the patch interface, and its factorization is reused as long as the patch remains fixed. The phase field is frozen in the exterior, introducing only a small approximation in the crack wake. The method is implemented in FEniCSx and evaluated for quasi-static crack propagation, dynamic crack branching, three-dimensional mixed-mode crack growth, and coalescence of multiple cracks in a unit cell. Across these problems, the condensed formulation reproduces the reference solutions with differences in global quantities below 0.5%, while substantially reducing the number of active degrees of freedom. In the quasi-static surfing problem, wall time speedups increase from 6.9 to 22.8 as the domain size is doubled, demonstrating increasing computational advantage for large-scale phase-field fracture simulations.

infographic.key_insight: Localizing repeated phase-field fracture solves to an adaptive crack-tip patch preserves reference accuracy while substantially reducing computational cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach makes large-scale brittle-fracture simulations more practical by concentrating resolution and solution effort near advancing cracks.
method: Adaptively refine and coarsen the mesh around active crack-tip patches.
Condense the inactive exterior onto the patch interface using a Schur complement, reusing its factorization while the patch stays fixed.
Freeze the exterior phase field and implement the localized formulation in FEniCSx.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across quasi-static, dynamic branching, 3D mixed-mode, and crack-coalescence tests, global quantities differed from reference solutions by less than 0.5%; surfing-test speedups rose from 6.9× to 22.8× when domain size doubled.
infographic.watch_item: Freezing the exterior phase field introduces a crack-wake approximation; patch updates must capture evolving fracture activity.
infographic.paper_title: Adaptive Crack-Tip Localization of Phase-Field Fracture Computations

title: Time to Fake It: Continual Machine Learning Intensifies Unfairness in Deepfake Detection
authors: Kajaree Das, Oliver Böse, Subarnaduti Paul, Gabriel Storch, Martin Mundt
abstract: Deepfake detectors safeguard against misinformation, rendering their failures as much a societal as a technical concern. As generators constantly evolve, detectors trained on static datasets miss newly arising threats, while progressive training interferes catastrophically. Yet, mitigating forgetfulness in terms of accuracy, the prevalent focus of continual learning (CL), is insufficient to reflect real-world impact. We therefore scrutinize the effects of CL methods with respect to evolving fairness. To this end, we analyze four dimensions of fairness across diverse demographics for detectors trained progressively on a chronological sequence of 11 real-world deepfake generation methods. Tracking fairness metrics over time, we expose non-trivial interplays between performance and fairness that depend on both the choice of CL algorithm and demographic intersections. We find accuracy degradation to typically exacerbate unfairness and, conversely, fairness improvements to remain scarce over time. Dissecting the CL method families (rehearsal, prompts, regularization), we observe that inequitable forgetting is not explained by underrepresentation alone, but likely entangled with representation learning. We thus issue a call to action for CL methods to take social outcomes into account when balancing the stability-plasticity tradeoff.

infographic.key_insight: Continual learning can intensify demographic unfairness in deepfake detection, and preserving accuracy alone does not ensure equitable outcomes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers deploying evolving deepfake detectors should monitor demographic fairness alongside accuracy and forgetting; this study does not directly address solid mechanics.
method: Train detectors progressively on a chronological sequence of deepfake generation methods.
Track four fairness dimensions across demographic groups and intersections.
Compare rehearsal-, prompt-, and regularization-based continual learning methods.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluation across 11 real-world deepfake generation methods found that accuracy degradation typically exacerbated unfairness, while fairness improvements remained scarce over time.
infographic.watch_item: Underrepresentation alone did not explain inequitable forgetting; the suggested role of representation learning requires further investigation.
infographic.paper_title: Time to Fake It: Continual Machine Learning Intensifies Unfairness in Deepfake Detection

title: Modeling Transport and Mechanics in Anion Exchange Membranes to Optimize Continuous CO2 Separations
authors: Samaneh Bayati, Jennifer Wade, Sara Sarbaz, Heidi Feigenbaum, Horacio Lopez-Marques, Winston Wang
abstract: Water transport in charged polymer membranes is strongly influenced by hydration-dependent transport properties and polymer-network deformation. Under water-activity gradients, spatial variations in water concentration induce swelling and mechanical stresses, while the resulting deformation can influence water transport. Capturing this bidirectional interaction is important for predicting membrane behavior under nonuniform hydration conditions. This study develops a transient finite element model of water transport and mechanical deformation in a Fumasep FAA-3-50 anion exchange membrane. The framework incorporates concentration-dependent water diffusivity, hygroscopic swelling, and nonlinear viscoelastic polymer response. Uncoupled, one-way coupled, and fully coupled formulations are compared to distinguish the effects of hydration-dependent diffusivity and mechanical coupling. In the fully coupled model, local water concentration governs swelling and mechanical response, while deformation, evolving membrane geometry, and mechanical pressure feed back into water transport. Simulations predict spatially and temporally nonuniform swelling and deformation that track the evolving water-concentration field. Relative to the uncoupled concentration-dependent diffusion model, mechanical feedback alters the predicted transport response, although transport remains primarily diffusion-driven. The fully coupled model is validated against steady-state water-transport measurements across water-activity gradients and reproduces the experimentally observed hydration dependence, with strongest agreement at intermediate hydration levels. These results highlight the importance of coupled hydration, swelling, deformation, and transport processes in models of hydrated anion exchange membranes and provide a framework for evaluating membrane behavior in moisture-facilitated transport applications.

infographic.key_insight: Hydration-dependent diffusion drives water transport in anion exchange membranes, while swelling and mechanical feedback modify the transport response.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Coupled transport–mechanics modeling can inform membrane design for continuous CO2 separations under nonuniform hydration.
method: Transient finite element modeling of Fumasep FAA-3-50 with concentration-dependent water diffusivity.
Hygroscopic swelling and nonlinear viscoelasticity coupled to water transport.
Comparison of uncoupled, one-way coupled, and fully coupled formulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The fully coupled model reproduces the hydration dependence of steady-state water-transport measurements, with strongest agreement at intermediate hydration levels.
infographic.watch_item: Validation reported in the abstract is steady-state; transient deformation predictions and performance at hydration extremes need further assessment.
infographic.paper_title: Modeling Transport and Mechanics in Anion Exchange Membranes to Optimize Continuous CO2 Separations

title: Geometric multigrid preconditioners for unfitted discretisations of the de Rham complex
authors: Santiago Badia, Jordi Manyer
abstract: We propose two families of multigrid preconditioners for unfitted finite element discretisations of the Riesz maps of the de Rham complex, in H(grad), H(curl) and H(div), stabilised by cell aggregation. The first is a geometric multigrid method applied directly to the unfitted operators, on a hierarchy of background meshes that share the same boundary representation. Its smoothers are star patches built on the aggregated mesh, so that each patch captures the kernel of the stabilisation. The second is a multilevel auxiliary-space preconditioner that combines a patch smoother localised around the cut cells with the body-fitted problem on the active mesh, which is in turn solved by a non-nested geometric multigrid method. Both are used as building blocks of block-diagonal preconditioners for the mixed Hodge Laplacians. Numerical experiments in two and three dimensions, on geometries with a controlled cut fraction and on general geometries, show iteration counts that are robust with respect to the cut configuration, the mesh size and the number of levels. We also report results for higher-order discretisations, weakly imposed Dirichlet boundary conditions and a face-based stabilisation.

infographic.key_insight: Two geometric multigrid preconditioner families deliver robust iteration counts for aggregation-stabilised unfitted finite element discretisations of the de Rham complex.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These solvers support efficient simulation on meshes that need not conform to complex boundaries, with applications to scalar and vector PDEs.
method: Apply multigrid directly to unfitted operators using background mesh hierarchies and aggregation-aware star-patch smoothers.
Combine cut-cell patch smoothing with an auxiliary body-fitted problem solved by non-nested geometric multigrid.
Use both approaches in block-diagonal preconditioners for mixed Hodge Laplacians.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments in 2D and 3D report iteration counts robust to cut configuration, mesh size and level count, with additional tests of higher order, weak Dirichlet conditions and face-based stabilisation.
infographic.watch_item: Implementation requires carefully designed patch smoothers and mesh hierarchies; robust iteration counts alone do not establish low setup cost or wall-clock scalability.
infographic.paper_title: Geometric multigrid preconditioners for unfitted discretisations of the de Rham complex

title: A Finite Element Method for the Surface Biharmonic Problem without Stabilization or Piola Transforms
authors: Jiachen Gu, Xia Ji, Shuo Zhang
abstract: For the biharmonic problem on closed smooth surfaces, we construct a nonconforming finite element method that requires neither stabilization nor the Piola transform. The reduced enriched quartic (REQ) element relies solely on vertex values and scalar edge moments. The same local construction applies to every triangle of a piecewise planar surface. The bilinear form consists of elementwise Laplacian inner products and permits standard finite element assembly. By separating the planar vertex residual from the angle defect contribution, we establish weak discrete Miranda--Talenti-type estimates on both planar meshes and closed piecewise planar surfaces. These estimates guarantee uniform stability on sufficiently refined interpolating surface meshes. We prove the well-posedness of the method, first-order convergence in the energy norm, and second-order convergence in the broken $H^1$ and $L^2$ norms. Numerical tests on three surfaces show the predicted convergence rates and examine the discrete Miranda--Talenti constants and angle defect scaling.

infographic.key_insight: A nonconforming finite element method solves biharmonic problems on closed smooth surfaces without stabilization or Piola transforms.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach simplifies finite element implementation for fourth-order surface equations through scalar degrees of freedom and standard assembly.
method: Use reduced enriched quartic elements with vertex values and scalar edge moments.
Assemble elementwise Laplacian inner products on piecewise planar surface triangles.
Establish stability using weak discrete Miranda–Talenti estimates that separate planar vertex residuals from angle defects.
infographic.evidence_signal: Analysis proves first-order energy-norm and second-order broken H1- and L2-norm convergence; numerical tests on three surfaces confirm the predicted rates and examine stability constants and angle-defect scaling.
infographic.watch_item: Uniform stability is guaranteed on sufficiently refined interpolating meshes of closed smooth surfaces; applicability beyond these assumptions is not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: A Finite Element Method for the Surface Biharmonic Problem without Stabilization or Piola Transforms

title: Co2In: a Bi-level Memory Incremental Learning Framework with Knowledge Encoding, Consolidation, and Integration
authors: Wenju Sun, Qingyong Li, Boyang Li, Wen Wang, Siyu Zhang, Yi Wei
abstract: Incremental learning (IL) aims to continually acquire new knowledge (plasticity) while retaining previously learned information (stability). However, striking a balance between plasticity and stability remains a significant challenge for intelligent systems. The human brain achieves exceptional balance, owing to various memory units that collaboratively encode and store information. Inspired by human memory mechanisms, this paper introduces an IL framework with knowledge enCoding, Consolidation, and Integration (Co2In). Co2In is designed as a bi-level memory architecture: a working memory for adaptive knowledge acquisition and a long-term memory dedicated to the persistent retention of information. The two memory modules work cooperatively during IL. The working memory first learns from new data to encode knowledge into parameters. Subsequently, Co2In performs a consolidation process to identify underlying patterns in the learned parameters and re-express them into a compact knowledge representation. Next, the knowledge representation and the identified patterns are transformed into separate network layers and integrated into the long-term memory. These designs empower Co2In to accumulate knowledge with high plasticity and stability. We evaluate Co2In on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet under exemplar-free Class-IL and Task-IL settings. Experimental results show that Co2In achieves state-of-the-art performance with efficient memory consumption.

infographic.key_insight: Co2In separates adaptive learning from persistent storage using working and long-term memory to balance acquisition of new knowledge with retention of prior knowledge.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could inform continually updated engineering AI models, but the abstract provides no solid-mechanics or constitutive-modeling validation.
method: Encode new knowledge in working-memory network parameters.
Consolidate parameter patterns into a compact knowledge representation.
Transform representations and patterns into separate layers integrated into long-term memory.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluations on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Tiny-ImageNet under exemplar-free Class-IL and Task-IL report state-of-the-art performance with efficient memory consumption.
infographic.watch_item: Memory growth across long task sequences and transfer to mechanics applications require further validation.
infographic.paper_title: Co2In: a Bi-level Memory Incremental Learning Framework with Knowledge Encoding, Consolidation, and Integration

title: Wavelength-selective bidirectional plasticity in self-powered Se/ZnMgO visual synapses
authors: Zacharie Jehl Li-Kao, Miho Akasaka, Myeongok Kim, Kunal J. Tiwari, Antoine Moore, Mykhailo A. Koltsov
abstract: Artificial visual synapses combine sensing, memory and processing in a single device, but most of them need an external voltage to read the synaptic weight and light is generally able to strengthen the weight rather than to weaken it. We report here Se/ZnMgO thin film photodiodes in which the photocurrent at zero bias writes and reads the synaptic weight, with a direction of change set by the photon energy alone. At equal photon flux, 365 nm pulses increase the photocurrent by 38 % while 455 nm pulses decrease it, and the depression reaching 30 % at higher flux, with up to 19 distinguishable levels per branch and no electrical energy spent. Spectrally resolved light soaking shows that short wavelengths potentiate while low-energy light erases. The interesting property is therefore the photon energy-dependent competition between potentiation and depression, the crossover being set by the defect population of the interface. Optical simulations show that both wavelengths are absorbed within the first tens of nanometres of Se, and the stored state is erased by a reverse bias in a voltage-dependent way and by sub-gap light, which indicates that potentiation corresponds to interface defects filled with electrons, in agreement with drift-diffusion simulations. The devices also show relearning, their response is modulated by bending on flexible substrates, and a network built from the measured weight updates reaches 89 % accuracy on handwritten digit recognition without noise and 85 % with the measured noise, against 97.5 % for floating-point weights.

infographic.key_insight: Self-powered Se/ZnMgO visual synapses use photon energy to increase or decrease synaptic weight at zero bias.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These photodiodes integrate optical sensing, memory and processing, offering a route to low-electrical-power neuromorphic vision on flexible substrates.
method: Apply wavelength-selective light pulses to write and read zero-bias photocurrent states.
Probe interface charge trapping using spectral illumination, reverse-bias erasure and device simulations.
Evaluate measured weight updates and noise in a handwritten-digit recognition network.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports 38% potentiation at 365 nm, depression reaching 30% at higher flux, up to 19 levels per branch, and recognition accuracy of 89% without noise and 85% with measured noise versus 97.5% for floating-point weights.
infographic.watch_item: The switching crossover depends on interface defects, making defect control important for reproducibility; zero electrical bias does not eliminate optical energy costs.
infographic.paper_title: Wavelength-selective bidirectional plasticity in self-powered Se/ZnMgO visual synapses

title: Plastic Flow Rule Based on Dislocation Link Velocity
authors: Hanfeng Zhai, Sh. Akhondzadeh, Ryan B. Sills, Nicolas Bertin, Wei Cai
abstract: We develop a theory for the plastic shear rate $\dotγ_i$ on each slip system $i$ of face-centered cubic (FCC) single crystals, by integrating the shear rate contributions $\dotγ_i(l)$ from dislocation links of length $l$. A generalized Orowan equation expresses $\dotγ_i(l)$ in terms of the link density $n_i(l)$ and the average link velocity $v_i(l)$. This model accurately reproduces the discrete dislocation dynamics (DDD) shear-rate data for all 12 slip systems across 99 loading orientations. In particular, it explains why the plastic shear rate depends exponentially on the resolved shear stress $τ_i$, as reported previously, in the absence of any thermally activated mechanism. This dependence arises from the exponential tail of $n_i(l)$ filtered through the threshold-like velocity function $v_i(l)$. Furthermore, $v_i(l)$ is well approximated by a single two-dimensional function $v(τ_i,l)$ for all these slip systems. The link velocity is therefore governed mainly by $τ_i$ and $l$, with only a minor effect from the complex interactions between slip systems. These interactions instead manifest themselves mainly through $n_i(l)$. As a demonstration of the effect of the link-length distribution on the slip rate, we show that even when $τ_i$ is limited to a narrow window, the shear rates still span two orders of magnitude. The supply of long links is therefore the dominant factor controlling slip-system activity, outweighing the direct effect of $τ_i$ on the link velocity.

infographic.key_insight: Long-link availability dominates slip-system activity, while an exponential link-length distribution filtered by threshold-like link velocities explains exponential stress dependence without thermal activation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model offers a microstructure-informed plastic flow rule for FCC single crystals that accounts for link-length distributions rather than relying on resolved shear stress alone.
method: Integrate length-resolved dislocation-link contributions using a generalized Orowan equation.
Represent average link velocity with a shared function of resolved shear stress and link length.
Capture most slip-system interaction effects through the link-length distribution.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model accurately reproduces DDD shear-rate data for all 12 slip systems across 99 loading orientations; rates span two orders of magnitude even within a narrow stress window.
infographic.watch_item: Practical use requires reliable link-length distributions; validation reported in the abstract is limited to FCC single-crystal DDD data.
infographic.paper_title: Plastic Flow Rule Based on Dislocation Link Velocity

title: Distributional signatures of computation: inferring mechanisms from computation time distributions
authors: Céline van Valkenhoef, Catherine Schuman, Nikolaus Kriegeskorte, Philip Walther
abstract: Computational complexity theory provides a framework for analysing abstract models of computation, whereas computational systems operate as finite physical implementations whose behaviour is shaped by their architecture and physical substrate. In such systems, computational organisation cannot be directly characterised from algorithms or internal representations. Building on the use of reaction time distributions to constrain mechanisms in cognitive science, we introduce an empirical framework for investigating computation in physical systems by inferring computational mechanisms from observable computation time distributions. The framework combines empirical benchmarking, which characterises computational efficiency through the scaling of computation time with problem size, with distributional analysis, which treats computation time distributions as signatures of the stochastic dynamics generated by different computational mechanisms. We demonstrate the framework using a scalable visual search paradigm, comparing human performance with three computational models that employ distinct mechanisms of evidence accumulation. Benchmarking reveals broadly similar scaling behaviour for the models and human observers, whereas distributional analysis distinguishes between these models. We show that computation time distributions provide an empirical level of description linking observable computational behaviour to underlying computational mechanisms. This framework complements computational complexity theory by extending the empirical study of computation from measuring computational performance to characterising computational organisation. It provides an empirical approach for comparing finite computational systems across diverse physical implementations, including biological, classical, neuromorphic, and quantum systems, without requiring access to their internal algorithms or architectures.

infographic.key_insight: Computation time distributions can distinguish computational mechanisms even when average time scaling appears broadly similar.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could support black-box comparison of finite computing systems across physical implementations, though solid-mechanics applications are not demonstrated.
method: Benchmark computation time as problem size increases.
Analyse time distributions as signatures of underlying stochastic dynamics.
Compare human visual search with three evidence-accumulation models.
infographic.evidence_signal: In a scalable visual search task, humans and models showed broadly similar time scaling, while distributional analysis distinguished the three models.
infographic.watch_item: Validation is limited to visual search; applicability to other tasks and physical computing platforms remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Distributional signatures of computation: inferring mechanisms from computation time distributions
